The Four Helpers

High Blood Pressure and Diabetes · Lesson 2

The Four Helpers

A flipchart for Care Group meetings. Show the picture side to the group. Turn to the text side to read the story, the questions and the messages.

  • Next and Back, or a swipe, turn the page.
  • Tap a picture to make it fill the screen.
  • Text shows what the facilitator reads. Picture goes back.

Lesson 2 at a glance

90 minutes. Bring the attendance registers and this flipchart. No materials are needed from the Activity Leader.

SectionMinutes
1. Game: The Sun Shines On5
2. Attendance and troubleshooting10
3 and 4. Story and questions Picture 2.110
5. Check Your Numbers; Eat Well and Move More Picture 2.210

Total90

Before the pictures

Recall Lesson 1. Ask the group to recall the key messages: the conditions are common; they are not a curse; you cannot catch them; you can feel well and still have them; the only way to know is to be checked.

Commitments. Ask: “What was your commitment at the last lesson? Have you been able to keep it?”

After the pictures

The Four Helpers Game. Teach one hand sign for each Helper. Say the words and do the sign together.

  • Check your numbers: wrap one hand around the other arm above the elbow, the way the blood pressure cuff does.
  • Eat well and move more: bring one hand to the mouth as if eating, then march on the spot.
  • Take your medicine every day: put a pretend tablet in the mouth and drink from a pretend cup.
  • Help each other at home: link arms with the person on each side.

Practise all four in order, three times. Then call out any Helper in any order, and let two or three participants take a turn as the caller. Ask: “Abena asked her mother, ‘What should I change in the kitchen?’ And what should Uncle Kofi change? What can we tell them now?”

Remind participants: no single Helper is enough. Good food and movement do not replace medicine that the health worker has given.

Discuss barriers. Ask: “Is there anything that might prevent you from using the Four Helpers?”

Request commitments. Ask: “Based on what you have heard today, what commitment will you make?” Each person chooses. Do not press anyone who is not ready.

Picture 2.1Story: Naa Goes to the Mission Hospital

Picture 2.1 · text sideStory: Naa Goes to the Mission Hospital

Read the story aloud.

Auntie Naa goes to the mission hospital. The nurse checks her blood pressure again. It is still high. The doctor gives her medicine. The nurse gives her a small card with her numbers on it.

Naa asks, “When I finish this medicine, will the BP be gone?” The nurse says, “No. The BP will stay with you. But you can control it. Four things will help you.”

At home, Uncle Kofi looks at the tablets. “So you will swallow these every day? Me, I take my medicine only when I feel the sugar.”

Their daughter Abena is cooking. She hears everything. She asks, “Mama, what should I change in the kitchen?” Naa does not know yet.

Ask the group.

  • What did the nurse tell Naa about her BP?
  • Kofi takes his medicine only when he “feels the sugar”. What do you think about that?
  • What do you do now to control your condition?

Encourage discussion. Do not correct “wrong” answers. Let everyone give an opinion. This page is for discussion, not for teaching.

Say “Let us compare your ideas with the messages on the following pages.”

Picture 2.2Check Your Numbers; Eat Well and Move More

Picture 2.2 · text sideCheck Your Numbers; Eat Well and Move More

Ask: “What do you think these pictures mean?” Affirm the answers. Then share each message.

You can control high blood pressure and diabetes. Four Helpers work together.

A

Helper 1. Check your numbers.

  • Go for your checks at the health facility. Keep every visit.
  • Know your blood pressure and your sugar. Keep your card.
B

Helper 2. Eat well and move more.

  • Use less salt, less sugar and less oil. Eat more vegetables.
  • Walk or move your body every day.

Ask the group.

  • Which of these two Helpers do you already use?
  • What makes it hard to keep your clinic visits?
Additional information for the facilitator

The Four Helpers are the frame for the whole module. Lessons 3 to 6 cover checking. Lessons 7 to 16 cover food, activity and habits. Lessons 17 to 21 cover medicine and clinic care. Lessons 22 to 24 cover preventing harm. Family support runs through every lesson and is the subject of Lesson 25.

Link to Value-Based Care. The VBC evaluation asks patients about three behaviours: reducing salt, keeping appointments and taking medicine. Helpers 1, 2 and 3 cover these.

Numbers. Do not teach target numbers today. Lesson 5 explains the two blood pressure numbers and the sugar number.

Picture 2.3Take Your Medicine Every Day; Help Each Other at Home

Picture 2.3 · text sideTake Your Medicine Every Day; Help Each Other at Home

Ask: “What do you think these pictures mean?” Affirm the answers. Then share each message.

A

Helper 3. Take your medicine every day.

  • Take it the way the health worker told you, even when you feel well.
  • Do not stop it or change it without asking the health worker.
B

Helper 4. Help each other at home.

  • The whole household eats the same healthy food.
  • Family members remind and encourage each other.
C

For most people, these conditions stay for life. With the Four Helpers, you can live long and well.

Ask the group.

  • Which of the Four Helpers is hardest for you?
  • Who at home can help you?
Additional information for the facilitator

“Cure”. Participants may have heard that a herb, a drink or a prayer cures BP or sugar disease. Explain that the conditions are controlled, not cured, and that the numbers go up again when a person stops care. Only a health worker should change a medicine.

Control is possible. PharmAccess reported in November 2025 that about 54% of patients enrolled in Value-Based Care had consistently controlled blood pressure, against 6% in the general population.

Medicines. CGVs do not advise on which medicine or dose to take. If a participant asks about a medicine or a side effect, tell her to ask the health worker at her next visit, or sooner if she feels unwell.
